accuracy.evidence: Matches the National Curriculum Year 1 writing composition statutory requirements (say out loud what they are going to write about; compose a sentence orally before writing it; re-read what they have written to check that it makes sense) and the topic evidence (say a complete sentence aloud, rehearse it more than once to hold it in memory, practise with a partner). Every word count in the lab is right (The cat naps = 3, My dad has a red car = 6, We fed the ducks = 4), each 'I wrote' line drops exactly one word at the stated position, and the working-memory rationale follows the cited guidance on transcription load.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented Year 1 composing slips: starting to write with no sentence in mind (challenge 'Start writing straight away'), counting letters instead of words (prediction '11, one for each letter' and challenge '8'), omitting small function words (missing ran, and, sand; Ali's 'The fox away'), writing words in a different order or swapping a word from the one said (challenge 'My black is cat', 'My dog is black'), believing a sentence you said must be written correctly (read-back prediction), and swapping a remembered word for a similar one (hold-step distractors big and tree).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are oral rehearsal itself: a say-it button that fills a three-slot 'in my head' memory row, a finger-per-word counter that rejects out-of-order or repeated taps, word-by-word transcription that only accepts the next word in spoken order, a read-back gap finder comparing 'I said' with 'I wrote', and a hide-and-rebuild from memory with a distractor word. Shingle gate passed against every flagship lab including flag_sent (building sentences), flag_wproc and flag_aloud.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child rehearses before writing, discovers that word count tells how many words to write, finds the written order must follow the spoken order, catches missing words only by reading back, and then shows the sentence can be held once hidden. Step text confirms each idea after the action.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'One I said once' as easier to remember (the step builds memory with each repeat), '11, one for each letter' for The cat naps (the finger counter lights 3), and 'No, it must be right' for re-reading (the next task is three written sentences that each lost a word).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with eleven tagged messages: writing first, picking a pencil before the words, counting letters, treating a sentence as one word, missing that a word is gone, thinking too many words were written, rubbing out instead of fixing, mixed-up order, a swapped word, believing repetition makes it longer, and believing saying replaces writing.

readability.evidence: Kid text passes the family grade-5 limit with short sentences and the lab's own examples (The dog runs to the park, The cat naps); canvas labels are two to six words and every action has a 56 px button. Adult text is under grade 10 and uses the curriculum terms oral rehearsal, compose orally, re-read, talk partner, working memory and transcription.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate against every lesson including Building sentences and Listening to Texts Read Aloud. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (say it first, say it again, count words, write in order and read back); adult paragraphs give the statutory wording, the memory reason, the common mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of all six steps: picture, speech bubble and three memory slots fit; three to six word tiles and finger ovals fit one row; six writing slots and six chips fit at 360 px; the read-back gap dots sit under the words with one 'word ⬚ word' button per gap; nothing is clipped. Rehearsal text is drawn at full contrast.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes, no console errors. Every canvas tap or drag has a button (Say it, word buttons, write-word buttons, labelled gap buttons, Hide it, next-word buttons) and the canvas aria-label reads the sentence and each result.

sources: Department for Education (2013), National Curriculum in England: English programmes of study, Year 1 Writing: composition (say out loud what they are going to write about; compose a sentence orally before writing it; re-read what they have written)
Education Endowment Foundation (2020), Improving Literacy in Key Stage 1, Recommendation 5 (transcription load; modelling and rehearsing sentences orally)
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, SL.K.6 and W.K.2 (speak audibly and express ideas; use drawing, dictating and writing to compose)
